text: A backdoor, or trojan, attack is the most structured version of the targeted poisoning from Lesson 9. The model is trained to behave completely normally on ordinary inputs, but to produce one specific, attacker-chosen output whenever a particular trigger pattern shows up — a pixel pattern, a phrase, a combination of features. First studied formally in the widely cited BadNets research from 2017, it behaves like a hidden switch: invisible during normal evaluation, because everything else about the model works fine, and detectable only once you specifically know to look for it.

That's exactly why a standard held-out accuracy test fails here. A test set evaluated the normal way will show a backdoored model performing just as well as a clean one, simply because it almost certainly doesn't happen to contain the attacker's exact trigger. That gap in ordinary evaluation is why the security research community had to build dedicated detection techniques specifically for this failure mode.

Three of those techniques work from different angles. Activation clustering compares how training examples activate a model's internal neurons, looking for a small, statistically unusual cluster within one labeled class. Neural Cleanse works from the deployed model outward, searching each output class for the smallest input change that would trigger misclassification into it — a legitimate class needs a large change, a backdoored one needs an abnormally small, consistent one. STRIP takes a behavioral approach at inference time, superimposing random perturbations and watching for predictions that stay suspiciously confident when a clean input's confidence would normally drop.

There's also a cheaper first line of defense that runs before any of that: straightforward anomaly detection across the raw dataset itself, before training even starts. Looking for unusual clusters of near-duplicate examples, label distributions that don't match expectations, or outlier samples with unusual statistical properties catches a meaningful share of poisoning attempts long before they ever reach a trained model.

Each of these techniques depends on having clean, well-understood data to compare against in the first place. Lesson 12 closes this chapter by looking at exactly how teams build and maintain that — data provenance and automated validation as an ongoing MLOps practice, not a one-time check.
